content.title: About
content.content: Crackers are thin, crunchy dry biscuits made from flour, water, and a small amount of fat. They are often enjoyed as a snack, a base for toppings, or as an accompaniment to soups and salads. Their texture is light and their flavor neutral, allowing them to pair well with a variety of spreads and dips.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Crackers originated in Europe in the 19th century as a way to extend the shelf life of bread.
There are many varieties, from plain salted to those flavored with herbs, cheese, or seeds.
In some cultures they are called "biscuits" and are used in traditional dishes such as Swiss fondue.
Thin crackers can be up to 90 % air, making them extremely light.
In the United States, "saltine" crackers are a popular small salted variety often served with soups.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Most crackers are made with minimal fat, making them less calorie‑dense than many baked goods.

items.title: Source of complex carbs
items.content: Crackers provide slowly released energy from complex carbohydrates, helping to maintain stable blood sugar levels.

items.title: Contains fiber
items.content: When made with whole‑grain flour, crackers can be a good source of dietary fiber that supports digestion.

items.title: Versatile platform for nutritious toppings
items.content: Crackers serve as a convenient base for adding protein (cheese, deli meat, hummus) and healthy fats (avocado, nut butter).

items.title: Low sugar content
items.content: Unlike many sweet biscuits, classic salted crackers contain virtually no sugar.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Traditional wheat‑based crackers may trigger reactions in people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: High sodium
items.content: Salted varieties often contain a lot of salt, which can be problematic for hypertension.

items.title: Limited nutrient density
items.content: Because of their simple composition, crackers can be low in vitamins and minerals unless fortified.

items.title: Risk of over‑eating
items.content: Their light texture encourages rapid consumption of large portions, increasing overall calorie intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Crackers can be eaten straight from the pack, spread with cream cheese, hummus, avocado, or used as a base for canapés. They are commonly served alongside soups, salads, and broths. For extra flavor, lightly toast them with herbs in the oven.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep crackers in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For longer storage, refrigerate them to prevent fat oxidation. Discard any crackers that become soft or develop a stale or moldy smell.

pastry-puff-custard-or-cream-filled-iced.title: Pastry, puff, custard or cream filled, iced or not iced

content.title: About
content.content: Pastries made from puff pastry with custard or cream filling are a popular dessert that can be glazed or left plain. The flaky dough gives a light, crisp texture, while the filling adds richness and flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Puff pastry originated in France in the 17th century and quickly became the basis for many baked goods.
Cream fillings are often based on pastry cream, custard, or whipped cheese.
Glazes can be chocolate, sugar, fruit, or simply a dusting of powdered sugar.
Traditionally these pastries are served with tea or coffee in European cafés.
Mini versions, sometimes called “croissant bites,” are popular in several countries.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: The puff pastry provides carbohydrates that supply quick energy.

items.title: B‑vitamin content
items.content: Dough made with eggs and milk contains B1, B2, and B6 vitamins important for metabolism.

items.title: Calcium from dairy
items.content: Cream fillings made with milk and butter deliver calcium beneficial for bones.

items.title: High sugar and fat
items.content: Glaze and buttery fillings make the pastries calorie‑dense; they should be enjoyed in moderation.

items.title: Allergy to dairy and eggs
items.content: Ingredients may trigger reactions in people with milk or egg intolerance.

items.title: Trans‑fat content
items.content: Using margarine in the dough can introduce trans fats, which are undesirable for heart health.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pastries can be enjoyed as a standalone dessert, served with tea or coffee, or used as a base for layered cakes. They are easy to cut into bite‑size portions.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 2 days. For longer keeping, refrigerate – up to 5 days. Bring to room temperature before serving so the dough stays tender.

content.title: About
content.content: Pumpkin seeds are the edible kernels of the pumpkin (Cucurbita pepo). They have a mild nutty flavor, a crunchy texture, and are often eaten raw or lightly roasted. Unsalted seeds are suitable for diet-conscious eating and are used in cooking, baking, and as a topping for dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pumpkin seeds have long been a staple in North American and Eastern European cuisines.
They are a good source of zinc, an essential mineral for immune function.
In ancient cultures, pumpkins and their seeds symbolized abundance and protection from evil spirits.
Pumpkin seeds are commonly used as bird feed and for small livestock.
Seeds can be green or yellow depending on the pumpkin variety.

items.title: Rich in zinc
items.content: Zinc supports immune health, wound healing, and DNA synthesis.

items.title: Contains magnesium
items.content: Magnesium aids muscle and nerve function and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Source of plant protein
items.content: Seeds provide essential amino acids needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Vitamin E and carotenoids protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports heart health
items.content: Polyunsaturated fatty acids help lower LDL cholesterol.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to pumpkin seeds.

items.title: High calorie density
items.content: Despite their benefits, seeds are calorie‑dense and should be consumed in moderation.

items.title: Phytic acid content
items.content: Phytic acid can reduce mineral absorption; soaking or roasting can mitigate this.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pumpkin seeds can be enjoyed as a snack, added to salads, yogurt, oatmeal, baked goods, or blended into a seed butter. They also make a crunchy topping for soups and stews. Soaking the seeds for a few hours and then drying them yields a softer texture.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store seeds in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. For longer shelf life, keep them in the refrigerator or freezer to prevent oil oxidation. Discard any seeds that develop a rancid smell.

content.title: About
content.content: A pepper‑flavored diet soft drink is a low‑calorie carbonated beverage that uses artificial sweeteners instead of sugar. It combines a subtle pepper heat with refreshing fizz, making it popular among fans of unconventional flavors and those watching their sugar intake.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The pepper aroma is obtained from red pepper extract, providing a mild spiciness without a burning sensation.
The diet version typically uses sucralose or stevia, keeping calories to 0–5 kcal per 100 ml.
Carbonated water enhances the perception of flavor and adds a crisp mouthfeel.
The drink is often marketed as “energy‑boosting” because capsaicin can slightly raise metabolism.
In some markets the product is sold in limited batches due to its niche taste profile.

items.title: Metabolism support
items.content: Capsaicin from pepper extract may modestly increase metabolic rate and aid calorie burning.

items.title: Low calorie
items.content: Being sugar‑free allows enjoyment without a significant increase in daily caloric intake.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: Carbonated water helps maintain fluid balance, especially in warm weather.

items.title: No sugar
items.content: Suitable for people with diabetes or those following low‑carb diets.

items.title: Antioxidant effect
items.content: Pepper extract contains small amounts of vitamin C and polyphenols with antioxidant properties.

items.title: Capsaicin sensitivity
items.content: Even mild spiciness can cause stomach discomfort or heartburn in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Artificial sweeteners
items.content: Excessive intake of sucralose or stevia may lead to gastrointestinal upset in some people.

items.title: Carbonation
items.content: Carbonated drinks can increase bloating and gas.

items.title: Pepper allergy
items.content: Rarely, an allergic reaction to pepper extract components may occur.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the drink chilled, straight from the bottle to preserve carbonation. It works as a refreshing snack between meals, a sugar‑free alternative to regular sodas, or as a base for non‑alcoholic cocktails.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the bottle in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. Once opened, consume within 3–5 days, sealing the cap tightly to maintain fizz and flavor.
